Vitastā
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda mentions the names of several rivers that were well-known during its period. There are 37 words in it which indicate a river. The Nadīstuti (Ṛgveda 10.7

) contains prayers addressed to ten rivers, out of which the वितस्ता is also one. It is described as a river having wet banks at a great height with the river flowing far below. It has been identified with the modern river Jhelum in the Punjab State.

Vitala
------------------------------------------
This nether world is just below अतल (See ATALA.).
Here शिव lives along with his wife Bhavāni and bhūtas (spirits and imps). His name is Hāṭakeśvara.
There is a river called Hāṭakī here.
Agni drinks its water. What he spits out becomes hāṭaka or gold.

vitaṇḍā
(‘cavil’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the kinds of debate mentioned in the Nyāyasūtras (

) of गोतम or गौतम (550 B. C.).
Here, the opponent does not try to establish his own position but goes on refuting that of the exponent. For all practical purposes it is destructive criticism. It is something like abusing the plaintiff’s lawyer when one has no case at all!

Vītahavya
------------------------------------------
A king of the solar race, he was the son of Śaryāti. He took refuge at the hermitage of the sage भृगु, performed austerities and became a ब्राह्मण. गृत्समद, a well-known sage, was his son.

vitarka
------------------------------------------
In general, the word means imagination or doubtful knowledge. However, the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) uses this word in a technical sense. It categorises samprajñātasamādhi (perfect concentration) into four varieties, the first one being with वितर्क (sa-वितर्क) (vide 1.17). Here वितर्क is defined as the intense awareness that arises in the मिन्द् when it concentrates on a gross object.
In another place (2.33.34) वितर्क is identified with certain obstacles to the practice of योग.

vitasti
(‘span’)
------------------------------------------
Vitasti seems to be a standard measure of length even from the oldest times (vide Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 13.7). It is described as of twelve aṅgulas.
Works on architecture and icono-graphy have defined this वितस्ति as the measurement of a span, the length between the tips of the thumb and the little finger when stretched. When this length is divided into twelve equal parts, each part is called an अङ्गुल. अङ्गुल is also the width of a finger. It is about three-fourths of an inch.
